text:
On the morning of February 12, 1966, Barbara Rosen woke before her alarm and lay in bed listening to the furnace, feeling the baby turn beneath her ribs the way a swimmer turns underwater—slowly, deliberately, with the whole weight of the body behind it. She was thirty-one and eight months pregnant, and she had decided the night before that she would go to Shabbat services no matter what her mother said. Her mother, who lived three blocks away in a brick ranch house identical to Barbara's own, had taken to calling every evening with a new reason Barbara should stay home. The roads were icy. The rabbi's sermons had been running long. It wasn't seemly, at a certain point, for a woman to be seen in shul looking like that.

But Barbara liked Rabbi Adler. Everyone liked Rabbi Adler—that was the thing people would say afterward, to the reporters, to the detectives, until the words wore smooth. He had come to the congregation in Southfield from Ohio six years earlier, when the suburb was still half fields and the synagogue was new enough that the mortar smelled of the trowel. He was tall, broad in the shoulders, with a voice that made the sanctuary feel smaller and warmer than it was. He had confirmed Barbara's older boy, Danny, the spring before, and had taken the trouble, at the reception afterward, to ask Danny about the model rockets he built in the basement, and Danny had talked about it for weeks.

That morning, Marty drove. He drove badly when he was nervous, and he was nervous most mornings now, with the baby coming and a new account at the agency. The streets were white at the edges with old snow, plowed and salted until it looked less like snow than like the residue of some industrial process. Marty said, "We could skip it. Nobody would say boo."

"I'm going," Barbara said.

The synagogue sat on a rise above the road, modern and low-slung, with a wall of tall windows the architect had intended to suggest the tents of the desert. Inside, the sanctuary was overheated and smelled of wool and wet galoshes. Barbara took her usual seat on the left, four rows back, and immediately regretted her coat, which she could no longer button and which trapped the heat against her like a held breath.

She noticed the young man during the second prayer, or perhaps the third—afterward she could never fix the moment, only the accumulation. He sat two rows ahead and to her right, in the aisle seat, young, nineteen or twenty, pale, dark-haired, wearing a suit that looked borrowed, the sleeves short enough to show an inch of wrist. He was not wearing a yarmulke, which was unusual but not remarkable; there were always visitors. What Barbara noticed was his stillness. Everyone else did the small restless choreography of services—rising, sitting, turning pages late and then too fast. The young man sat like a stone in a creek. His hands were in his lap. He did not hold a prayer book. Barbara thought: something is wrong with him. And then, because she was pregnant and tired and the rabbi was approaching the bimah, she thought nothing more about it.

Rabbi Adler began his sermon. It was about Abraham Lincoln—it was Lincoln's birthday, and the rabbi had a fondness for finding in the civic holidays a doorway into the older texts. He spoke about Lincoln's melancholy, about the idea that a great man might carry a private grief the way a city carries a river. Barbara had heard him preach maybe a hundred times, and she thought, shifting her weight, that this one was better than most. She remembered the phrase "the loneliness of the unburdened." She remembered the way the rabbi stood with one hand on the edge of the lectern, not gripping it, as though the lectern were a companion.

The young man stood up.

Barbara saw it from the side and slightly behind, a perspective that strips an event of its drama and leaves only its mechanics. He stood, and he walked down the aisle toward the bimah, and he was not hurrying. The ushers—two retirees named Sol and Hy—did not move, because there was nothing to move toward yet. The young man reached into his jacket. There was a sound, later described in the newspapers as a crack and by Barbara, in the one interview she gave and regretted, as "like a book dropped flat on a table," and Rabbi Adler put his hand to his chest with an expression not of pain but of mild surprise, the look of a man who has just remembered he left something on the stove. There was a second sound. The rabbi sat down on the steps of the bimah, in his black robe, as though he had simply decided to rest.

What Barbara remembered most clearly from the next thirty seconds was the silence, which had a texture to it, dense and granular, as though the sanctuary had been filled with sand. No one screamed at first. Later, everyone screamed. But first there was the silence, and in it the young man turned to face the congregation, and Barbara saw his face fully for the first time, and it was not twisted or wild—it was empty, smooth, almost serene, the face of someone who has finished a chore.

She stood up. She never could explain this to herself afterward, not to Marty, not to the detective, not to the rabbi's widow, who took her hand at the shiva house with a bewildered gratitude. She was eight months pregnant, and she stood up, and she began to move down the aisle toward the young man with the gun, with some half-formed idea in her body—her body thought it, not her mind—that she could reach him, that she could put her hand on his arm, that a woman in her condition was a kind of argument no one could answer. She got perhaps three steps. Sol was shouting "Get down, get down" in a voice that cracked upward like a boy's.

Then the crowd broke.

It was not a crowd when it broke; it became one in the breaking, five hundred people converted in an instant into a single animal with a hundred legs. Barbara felt herself carried sideways by shoulders and elbows and the hard corner of someone's prayer book, her feet touching the carpet only occasionally, the way a stone touches the water in a skipping throw. She heard the third shot as she was moving, muffled by the bodies around her, and she understood later that this was the one the young man saved for himself. Someone's hand closed on her upper arm and she thought, absurdly, that it was the shooter, and struck at it, and it was Marty, with Danny clutched under his other arm like a football, and then the cold air hit her face and they were outside, in the flat gray February light, and people were running across the parking lot and slipping on the ice.

Barbara stood with her hand on her belly and looked back at the wall of windows, the tents of the desert, and waited for the whole thing to reverse itself the way a film runs backward. Nothing came out of the doors except people, and then, after a while, the sirens.

The baby, a girl, was born on the second of March, two and a half weeks early, as though she had decided the world was in such a state that one might as well get on with it. They named her Ruth. Rabbi Adler's funeral had been held four days after the shooting, in the same sanctuary, and Barbara had not been allowed to go—Marty and her mother had formed an alliance on the matter—but she listened to the eulogies on the radio, holding Ruth in the hospital chair, the small hot weight of her, while outside the window the last of the February snow came down in slow, uncommitted flakes.

The young man's name was printed in the papers. He was twenty-one. He had been a student, briefly, and had been in and out of a hospital in Ann Arbor, and his parents issued a statement through a lawyer that used the word "incomprehensible" twice. There was talk for a while about locking the doors during the sermon, but it came to nothing, because no one could hold the shape of that morning in mind long enough to build anything from it.

Years later, when Ruth was grown and Danny's rockets were in a box in her own attic, Barbara would still sometimes dream the three steps she took down the aisle—dream them with the crowd frozen around her, and herself moving through it calmly, enormously pregnant, toward the still young man, her hand already rising to touch his sleeve. In the dream she always reached him. In the dream, that was the whole point: that you could reach someone, that the distance between two people in a sanctuary was never so great it couldn't be crossed in three steps, and that the worst thing that had ever happened to her was not the shots, or the crowd, or even the death of a good man on Lincoln's birthday, but the moment the world showed her otherwise, and swept her away.
